dialogue.text: [serious, engaging] Between 1929 and 1933, that thinking helped shrink world trade by about two thirds. And in Cairo, the baker raises his prices one more time, and this time a crowd forms outside his shop.
[serious, engaging] Month four, and finally, good news. Which is exactly when most people make their worst mistake.

[serious, engaging] The central banks, the banks that print each country's money, cut interest rates and promise to print as much as it takes. Stocks jump twenty percent in two weeks. Your fund climbs back to nine thousand, and on TV, everyone says the worst is over.

[serious, engaging] They said that in November 1929 too. America's stock market climbed almost fifty percent, then fell another eighty-six. And our rally dies the same way: Corvane's chips sell at auction for less than five thousand dollars each, two more AI companies miss payments, and your fund drops to six thousand dollars.

[quiet, direct] So be honest for a second. You've watched four thousand dollars disappear, you got your hopes up, and now it's gone again. Would you sell? Most people do. People who stayed calm through the first drop give up in the second and sell right near the bottom, and a loss on a screen becomes a real one. Hold on to your answer.
[serious, engaging] Which brings us to the question underneath all the others: is your money going to be worth anything?
[serious] In America, at first, it's worth more. Nobody is buying, so prices drop and every dollar buys more. During the Great Depression, prices in America fell by about a quarter.
